narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year class ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward not passing. Together, these two performance measures outweighed everything else. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential piece of information, but it worked in the opposite direction, giving a modest pull toward passing.

In practical terms, your first- and third-year rankings placed you in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average student who was admitted (around the sixth decile). Your LSAT score of 32 and undergraduate GPA of 3.0 were also below the typical admitted student, though your GPA still provided a small positive signal. Your middle-income background and plan to attend full-time are fairly common among admitted applicants and did not meaningfully affect the result.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking the LSAT, enrolling in a structured bar-preparation course, or spending time improving your study habits before reapplying. These steps can directly address the areas that most influenced this decision. (218 words)
